sections.normalized_html:
A quadratic equation has real solutions if the discriminant is non-negative: [MATH: \mathcal{D} \geq 0.]

First, rewrite the equation in standard quadratic form:

[MATH: x(5x − k)|= − 10; 5x^{2} − kx|= − 10; 5x^{2} − kx + 10|= 0]

The coefficients of our quadratic equation are the following:

[MATH: a = 5, \qquad b = -k, \qquad c = 10]

So, computing the discriminant, we get

[MATH: D|= b^{2} − 4ac; = (− k)^{2} − 4(5)(10); = k^{2} − 200.]

To have real solutions, we need [MATH: \mathcal{D} \geq 0{:}]

[MATH: k^{2} − 200|≥ 0; k^{2}|≥ 200; k|≥ sqrt(200)]

Since [MATH: k] must be positive, we conclude that the least possible value is [MATH: 10\sqrt{2}.]

sections.normalized_html:
For a quadratic equation [MATH: at^2 + bt + c = 0,] the discriminant is [MATH: \mathcal{D} = b^2 - 4ac.]

  • If [MATH: \mathcal{D} > 0,] there are two distinct real solutions.

  • If [MATH: \mathcal{D} = 0,] there is exactly one real solution.

  • If [MATH: \mathcal{D} < 0,] there are no real solutions (the solutions are complex).

The coefficients of our quadratic equation are the following: [MATH: a = 4, \qquad b = k, \qquad c = 36]

Computing the discriminant, we get

[MATH: D|= b^{2} − 4ac; = k^{2} − 4(4)(36); = k^{2} − 576.]

To have more than one real solution, we need [MATH: \mathcal{D} > 0{:}]

[MATH: k^{2} − 576|> 0; k^{2}|> 576; sqrt(k^{2})|> sqrt(576);|k||> 24]

Notice that among the given options, only [MATH: -26] satisfies this condition.

Therefore, [MATH: k = -26] is the correct answer.

sections.normalized_html: Given that [MATH: x(2x + 12) = -k,] where [MATH: k] is an integer constant, has two distinct real solutions, what is the greatest possible value of [MATH: k?]
sections.readable_text: Given that [MATH: x(2x + 12) = -k,] where [MATH: k] is an integer constant, has two distinct real solutions, what is the greatest possible value of [MATH: k?]

sections.normalized_html:
A quadratic equation has two distinct real solutions if the discriminant is positive: [MATH: \mathcal{D} > 0.]

First, rewrite the equation in standard quadratic form:

[MATH: x(2x + 12)|= − k; 2x^{2} + 12x|= − k; 2x^{2} + 12x + k|= 0]

The coefficients of our quadratic equation are the following:

[MATH: a = 2, \qquad b = 12, \qquad c = k]

So, computing the discriminant, we get

[MATH: D|= b^{2} − 4ac; = (12)^{2} − 4(2)(k); = 144 − 8k.]

To have distinct real solutions, we need [MATH: \mathcal{D} > 0{:}]

[MATH: 144 − 8k|> 0; 144|> 8k; 8k|< 144; k|< (144)/(8); k|< 18]

Since [MATH: k] must be an integer, we conclude that the greatest possible value is [MATH: 17.]

Item 2 — Example: Determining Parameter Values in Quadratic Equations With Real Solutions

b = -k, \qquad

Since [MATH: k] must be positive, we conclude that the least possible value is [MATH: 10\sqrt{2}.]
